HYDROGEN IRRADIATION-DRIVEN COMPUTATIONAL SURFACE CHEMISTRY OF LITHIUM OXIDE AND HYDROXIDE P.S. Krstic1,2,*, S. Dwivedi3, E.T. Ostrowski4, S. Abe5, A. Maan5, A.C.T van Duin3,  and B.E. Koel4

1TheoretiK, Port Jefferson Station, NY 11776, USA 2Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, New York 11749, USA 3Department of Mechanical Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802, USA 4Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA 5Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Princeton, NJ, USA ABSTRACT We have investigated, using molecular dynamics, the surface chemistry of hydrogen incident on the amorphous and crystalline lithium oxide and lithium hydroxide surfaces upon being slowed down by a collision cascade and retained in the amorphous surface of either Li2O or LiOH. We looked for the bonding of H to the resident structures in the surface to understand a possible chain of chemical reactions that can lead to surface transformation upon H atom impact. Our findings, using Density- Functional Theory (DFT) trained ReaxFF/EEM potentials, stress the importance of inclusion of polarization in the dynamics of a Li-O-H system, which is also illustrated by DFT energy minimization and quantum-classical molecular dynamics using DFTB. The resulting polar-covalent chemistry of the studied systems is complex and very sensitive to the instantaneous positions of all atoms as well as the ratio of concentrations of various resident atoms in the surface. \ *Corresponding author: krsticps@gmail.com

1. INTRODUCTION There is a high interest in the fusion energy community in lithium (Li) coating of the plasma-facing components (PFCs) of fusion devices. Primary reasons for this interest include the reduction of hydrogen (H) recycling and the suppression of Edge Localized Modes (ELMs) and other plasma disruptions in the edge plasma. Li coatings chemically retain H and background vacuum impurities, which can yield a lowrecycling regime that is characterized by lowering recycled H atoms (or molecules). Recycled H atoms are defined as H atoms (or ions) that are incident on the wall and either reflect or desorb from the wall at lower energy. In a low-recycling regime, the plasma edge temperatures can remain at a high fraction of the core values [1,2]. The low-recycling regime requires a recycling coefficient below 0.5, which is the ratio of reflected atomic and recombined molecular hydrogen fluxes to the impinging ion flux [3]. Under these circumstances, the cooling of the plasma edge is lessened, suppressing steep temperature gradients that can induce instabilities. Many tokamaks have used Li coatings [4-10] and observed improvements in plasma performance. Due to better control of edge plasma pressure, MHD (Magneto-Hydro-Dynamical) instabilities can also be minimized, avoiding disastrous events for tokamak reactors, such as Edge- Localized Modes (ELMs) or disruptions, that produce peak power loads on the divertor plates [11]. Thus, the key processes at the surfaces of the Li-coated PFCs are reflection and its complement, retention. An experimental finding shows Li is volumetrically converted into lithium-deuteride if the D fluence is high enough (LiD) [12]. Notably, the D recycling depends on the near-surface chemical content. Experiments on thin lithium films also observed the hydrogen retention effect and showed that H is retained in Li and Li2O with similar efficiency but by different mechanisms [13]. Experiments of Taylor et al. [14-17] on lithium films intercalated into carbon demonstrated that with a significant D fluence, oxygen concentration near the surface of these samples could increase up to 40%. Modeling by Krstic and coworkers of these systems indicated hydrogenic fuel retention could be strongly affected by the presence of oxygen [15], showing that oxygen could be a main player in bonding with the impact deuterium, rather than Li if the concentration of oxygen in graphite becomes comparable to that of lithium. Their work involved the use of advanced computational atomistic simulations using classical molecular dynamics (CMD) and quantum-classical molecular dynamics (QCMD) to explain a subtle interplay of Li, B, C, O, and D chemistry inside the irradiated surface, resulting in sputtering and D reflection and retention, as well as energy, angular and mass spectra of ejected atoms and molecules from the surfaces [18-25]. They also showed that erosion of carbon can be significantly reduced by the presence of oxygen, boron, and lithium. Validation was carried out by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements in laboratory experiments and with the Material Analysis Particle Probe (MAPP) of borontreated graphite samples introduced in the NSTX-U divertor region and exposed to D plasmas [24-31]. Future fusion reactors will not be equipped with carbon walls but high-Z metals, like tungsten, or their alloys. Lithium does not intercalate in such materials. The thickness of Li coatings on high-Z substrates can be on the scale of hundreds of nm, while the penetration of H in Li and Li compounds is smaller than 20 nm for H impact energies smaller than 100 eV [32]. Therefore, it is reasonable to study the plasma-material interactions of just the Li compound overlayer in many cases, irrespective of its high- Z substrate. Since the coating is often carried out by evaporative deposition, the coated layers are amorphous, whether they are solid or liquid. However, the lithium coatings can quickly oxidize to form lithium oxide, Li2O, and lithium hydroxide, LiOH, owing to the presence of water in the background gas of the vacuum vessel and oxygen from oxide components and oxidized metal PFCs. This Li oxidation may have happened before or in parallel with the creation of LiH. Recent classical molecular dynamics using ReaxFF Force Field (CMD/ReaxFF) studies of Krstic and coworkers [32-35] computed the effects of irradiation of crystalline and amorphous Li, LiH, LiOH, and Li2O by hydrogen atoms and its isotopes at various incident angles and energies (0.05–100 eV). These studies considered interatomic polarization effects due to the low electronegativity of Li (0.95) and the high electronegativity of O (3.4) in comparison to H, which is one of the distinctive features of MD with lithium materials and oxygen involved. They showed that complex chemistry emerges upon impinging a hydrogen atom into Li or Li compound surfaces, with the reaction mechanisms depending on the

They determined that the recycling coefficient (RC) of H at 0o incident angle and 100 eV is about 2.5 times smaller for an amorphous LiH surface than for an amorphous Li surface, while the RC is about 2.7 times smaller for an amorphous Li2O surface compared to LiH. The RC for LiOH is only 20% smaller than that for Li. All these ratios are dependent on impact energy, especially for Li2O.  The penetration of H into LiH is smaller than into Li, due to energy loss in H-H collisions. The probability of sputtering of Li at normal incidence of H does not exceed 1% for any of the studied Li compounds (LiH, LiOH, Li2O) in the considered energy range, while the probability of sputtering of H achieves 5-10%. At almost grazing incidence, the sputtering of Li increases, reaching 6%. The energies of the sputtered Li increase with the impact energy, reaching about 10 eV for impact of H of 100 eV. The depth of the retained particles does not exceed 10 nm for LiOH and decreases with impact angle and isotopic mass but is smaller for LiH and Li2O. These values are significantly smaller than those of 15 nm for pure Li, which has the smallest mass density (0.5 g/cm3). We note that several differences in probabilities of various processes diminish for almost all grazing incidences. These earlirer studies show the importance of understanding the regime of low-impact energies (<100 eV) in a plasma. This range of energies is the richest with various processes, producing a variety of sometimes unexpected effects in retention, reflection, and sputtering, ending with exciting chemical processes when impact particles are slowed in the material by a cascade of inelastic processes.  It is also important to use reactive classical potentials equipped with the ability to accurately consider polarization and charging of interacting atoms involving Li and O, as well as quantum methods of molecular dynamics in case we are interested in the chemistry of retained atoms or distinguishing the molecular products of the chemical sputtering. In order to understand the chemistry underlying the effects of increased retention of H in the oxidized Li materials and take initial steps in finding the optimal ratio of Li, O, and H for the lowest recycling, we have undertaken the present MD study. We looked for possible final chemical bonds of low-energy incident hydrogen that was retained in Li2O and LiOH surfaces. Since H creates polar-covalent bonds with both Li and O at the end of its collisional cascade, when it almost thermalizes with Li and O atoms in the slab, the prospective creation of the bonds might be highly sensitive to the accuracy of the atomic charges, dependent on the instantaneous coordinates of atoms in the slab. The ReaxFF family of reactive bond order potentials contain accurate interatomic energy functions for the Li-O-H systems developed and described in detail in our previous papers [32-35]. However, the dynamic charges used to describe polarization of atoms are calibrated with Electronegativity Equalization Method (EEM), which can exhibit inaccuracies due to unphysical long-range charge transfer issues [36,37]. On a separate note, due to the chemical complexity of Li-O-H systems, in this study, we do not pursue here the surface chemistry with accumulated hydrogen atoms irradiation instead, we apply many trajectories to the surface target and draw our conclusions based on the obtained statistics rather than on a single trajectory. We describe the computational methods in Section 2. In Section 3, we show our results and provide adequate comparisons and discussions. Our conclusions are shown in Section 4. 2. METHODS A need for a specific and careful investigation of the surface chemistry of Li and O compounds arises from the large difference in the electronegativities of Li and O to other constituents of the plasma-facing materials (PFCs). Atoms with higher electronegativities tend to accept electrons, while atoms with lower electronegativities tend to donate their electrons in chemical reactions. Consequently, with Li and O present in the surface, one can expect strong electrical polarizations of atoms, ionic compounds, and longrange Coulomb interactions. In our previous publications, we performed studies of sputtering, retention, reflection, and other processes for impacts of hydrogen and deuterium in the energy range 1-100 eV at Li surfaces containing H and/or O. Since polarization effects are built by atomic electrons, classical molecular dynamics (CMD) has to be replaced by a method that would effectively account for the changes in the atomic electron clouds dynamically while impact atoms and atoms, resident  in the surface, are moving. The most accurate method would be Quantum Classical MD (QCMD), treating the motion of nuclei classically while solving the electron dynamics by ab initio or at least by a first-principles quantum method, for example, DFT, which scales as N3, where N characterizes the system size. A less computationally intensive method would be QCMD using an approximation to DFT, for example, SCC-DFTB (scales as N2). Besides being limited to the systems of a smaller number of atoms, the approximations involved do not warrant its accuracy, and it may sometimes lead to wrong conclusions, as turns out to be the case here. The least computationally expensive method would be a CMD (scales as ~N), which dynamically calculates the charges of the atoms using an appropriate semi-empirical calibration (e.g., EEM). A prominent example of a classical force field combined with EEM is ReaxFF, implemented in the Large Scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) [38]. The final judge for the accuracy of these approaches would be adequate experimental results and, in some cases, the DFT energy considerations, like those involved in this study. While DFT calculations could be very accurate, they are also the most computationally intensive and can only handle systems of a few hundred atoms before becoming prohibitive and on a very limited temporal scale. DFT is useful for studying local interactions and for building the database for the training of classical potentials but not for simulating larger atomic systems for longer-range interactions, many trajectories needed for statistics, etc. For some of our test calculations, we employ the SCC-DFTB method [39, 40, 20] developed by the Bremen (Germany) Center for Computational Material Sciences. This method is a tight-binding approximation to DFT in which only valence orbitals are considered, and difficult density integrals are parameterized and fitted in advance. In comparison to other tight-binding methods, this one has a self-consistent calculation of atomic charges, which is critical for handling the*

Still, for the size of the systems and large number of trajectories, the scaling of N2 of this method presents a computationally formidable problem and can be used only for tests with significantly reduced system sizes. Parameterization of the Slater-Koster pair-potentials for the Li–C–O–H-W-B-Mo mixtures has been developed so far through our previous collaboration with other groups [15,20]. In this paper, we systematically use CMD with ReaxFF/EEM in order to get qualitative answers on how the impacting, retained hydrogen atoms modify the chemical content of a surface containing Li, O, and H. ReaxFF is a classical potential with the capability to correctly treat chemical processes in the material of interest [41, 42]. In ReaxFF, bonded energies (bond, angle, torsion, etc.) are described as a function of bond order, and the bond order is calculated as a function of interatomic distances. However, the non-bonded energies (van der Waals and electrostatic) are calculated as a function of atomic positions. The van der Waals energy is obtained from a distance-corrected Morse potential, and the electrostatic energy is calculated by shielded coulombic force [43]. To calculate the electrostatic force, the atomic charges are calculated by EEM. The ReaxFF force field parameters are generally trained by QM and/or experimental data and the parameters used in this work were developed and used for the Li, O, and H set of atoms in our previous publications [32 – 35]. Finally, to decide on the accuracy of the ReaxFF/EEM vs. DFTB calculations, we perform DFT calculations as a benchmark. We use the program package VASP for PWDFT calculations [44], and NWCHEM, for “molecular” DFT calculations with Gaussian bases [45]. We study in detail two generic surface targets frequently observed in LTX-β and other fusion reactors with liquid or solid lithium Plasma Facing Components (PFCs): lithium oxide (Li2O) and lithium hydroxide (LiOH).  For Li2O (Fig.1), a surface slab of dimensions 4.7x4.7x22.7 nm3, amorphized and thermalized to 300 K, and relaxed to the surface boundary conditions and 2D periodicity, contained about 30,000 atoms (i.e., 20,000 Li atoms and about 10,000 O atoms) with average inter-atomic distances of 2.56 Å, resulting in a correct mass density close to 2 g/cm3. These large slabs were analyzed by CMD using ReaxFF. Crystalline and amorphized slabs of Li2O and LiOH, having up to 1,100 atoms, were also created and used for detailed analysis. For DFT calculation, we used a Li2O crystal slab of 96 atoms with 26 H atoms embedded in it. For LiOH, an amorphized slab, 5.6x5.6x12.2 nm3 of density ~1.5 g/cm3, contained a total of 29,735 atoms (about 1/3 of each of Li, O, and H atoms), with average inter-atomic distances of 2.34 Å. Most of the Li2O and LiOH molecules were dissociated in the process of amorphization. All surface slabs were set to 300 K by the Langevin thermostat before bombardment by hydrogen, using damping constant of 100, followed by relaxation without thermostat, until the slab temperature was stabilized. The thermostat was not applied during the collisional cascade of hydrogen. The chemical reactions of the retained H (D) atoms are by far the most efficient when an impact atom thermalizes by a cascade of inelastic collisions with the atoms of the surface. Therefore, impact energy and angle of incidence are not expected to influence the chemical reactions of the impact atoms other than by dependence of the trajectory or retention depth on the impact parameters. Due to inhomogeneities in the surface, the target variation of the retention depth can cause slight variation in the results. In all calculations, we uniformly scan the surface area of the slab, open to the vacuum, by hundreds or thousands of non-accumulative impacts, emitting a particle toward the surface from a plane that is, in most cases, 10 Å above the surface. The time step in the calculations was variable (0.25 -0.5 fs), and the total number of steps was between one and ten thousand. All conclusions on the targeted chemistry were obtained as a statistical average over a large number of used trajectories. 3. We then applied DFT energy minimization of the system by applying DFT, with b3lyp hybrid functional and STO-3G continued by 6-31G** basis set, using NWCHEM computational chemistry package [45]. Like in Section 3.1.2A, we keep Li and O atoms fixed during the geometry optimization of H atoms, preventing change of the cluster shape.  This way, the system energy was minimized by allowing only hydrogen atoms to move.

The optimization converged with an interesting outcome (Fig. 10b). The H atoms close to the cluster center of the cluster moved away from the O atom, moving to a point where it is coordinated to 4+4 Li atoms and 2 O atoms, similarly to the final position of H in Fig. 8. All other H atoms moved toward the “surfaces”, either bonding to O, coordinating to only 4 Li atoms, or moving to the cluster borders.  At the surface, the coordination is generally lower than in the bulk, and H can bond also to O atoms. In the crystal bulk, each Li atom was coordinated to 4 O atoms, and each O atom was coordinated to 8 Li atoms. The layer of quasi-H-O-H was only partially stable. The artificially (initially) created H-O- H molecules at the cluster dissociated, and H moved in or out of surface. The O atoms at the surface were initially coordinated to 4 (rather than to 8) Li atoms, which allowed them to bond one or two H atoms. Therefore, H cannot bond to either Li or O in Li2O crystal bulk, but bonding to O is more probable at the top layer of the surface where the coordination number of O atoms is reduced. In the case of a:Li2O, H can bond by a hydrogen bonding (dipole-dipole interaction) to O atoms. However, the strength and prevalence of these interactions would depend on the specific properties of the a:Li2O material, such as its composition and structure, and would need to be evaluated case-by-case. It is important to stress that the above chemical behaviors of H atoms were common for both DFT (b) and the CMD/ReaxFF (c) calculations but not for DFTB calculations (d). The trajectories of the H atoms which  reflect dynamics of geometry optimization using DFT, ReaxFF and DFTB are shown in Supplementary Materials (SM2).

The DFTB calculations usually show increased bonding, which in this case is critical: All H atoms in the process of energy minimization stay bonded to local O atoms, only rotating around them rather than translating as in cases of (b) and (c). A detailed study of the statistics of surface chemistry in a small, amorphous Li2O slab, irradiated by a large number of 5 eV H was shown in SM3. The results are quite different than those of Fig.2: The distribution of the shortest distances of retained D to the slab atoms (SM3.2) shows a strong peak at about 1 Å, which is close to the bond length of an OD- radical (0.97 Å). There is also a small LiD peak at ~1.7Å, and a strong peak at d(Li-D) at ~2.3Å which could correspond to  V-shaped LiOD molecules. This is well corroborated by the distribution of charges of D, as illustrated in Figs. SM3.1 and SM3.3-SM3.5. CONCLUSIONS We studied the bonding chemistry of a hydrogen atom impinging on amorphous surface slabs of lithium oxide (Li2O) and lithium hydroxide (LiOH). We found that the polarization of atoms due to the high electropositivity and high electronegativity of Li and O, respectively, and the resulting charging of impact H (Him) (and surface H atoms (HS) in the case of LiOH) have a decisive role in creation of the polarcovalent bonds of Him with Li and O. An incorrect charge sign of Him could lead to wrong or incomplete predictions of its bonding chemistry and wrong conclusions about the H- irradiated slab structure. We performed calculations with CMD using ReaxFF, included comparisons with QCMD using SCC-DFTB, and verified findings with crystalline Li2O with two independent DFT calculations. We found that Him in amorphous Li2O (a:Li2O), calculated by CMD/ReaxFF, is consistently charged negatively, which hinders bonding of Him to O in the amorphous and crystalline slabs. In effect,*

even in the amorphous mixture of dissociated Li2O, Him is not bonded to either Li or O. In fact, the analysis of the effects in crystalline Li2O confirmed that H is neither bonding to surface atoms nor creating a compound. Rather, the incident H is retained in the potential minima of the typical multi-atom – multi-coordinated configurations. The results that were obtained in an amorphous Li-O slab are, in part, smeared “versions” of the effects of the atom configurations shown for the Li2O crystal. The DFT geometry optimizations of a number of “seeded” H atoms in a small, 2x2x2 superlattice of Li2O showed that H atoms close to the symmetry center of the lattice occupies a multi-coordinated potential minimum, similarly as found with the ReaxFF calculations in a Li2O crystal. However, some H atoms acquired a positive charge in the process of the DFT geometry optimization. Interestingly, the SCC-DFTB calculations give a different picture of the bonding chemistry of H in an  a:Li2O surface, in which  many H atoms get a positive charge and are bonded to the resident oxygen atoms, and only a few H atoms are bonded  to Li atoms, and some  possibly create V-shaped LiOH molecules. The DFT calculations with a Li2O crystal agree well with the ReaxFF results, while the DFTB calculations indicate that all H atoms get charged positive and strongly bond to oxygens. Thus, the potential field of ReaxFF leads to an acceptable description of the H chemistry, while DFTB leads, in this case, to a qualitatively wrong picture of the bonding interplay between H, Li and O. Obviously, the over-bonding potential field resulting from the existing Li-O-H pair potentials in DFTB is not accurate enough to create correct interparticle dynamics. Varying concentration ratios of O, Li, and H and observing resultant atomic charging indicate that the surface chemistry might also strongly depend on the proportion of the Li-O-H constituents. The importance of inclusion of atomic charging for the system chemistry is further stressed by the results of CMD/ReaxFF calculations with the exclusion of charges in LAMMPS. This leads to  completely different particle dynamics and an inadequate bonding chemistry. In spite of the current success of the ReaxFF potential, we see space for further improvement, as indicated by the DFT Li2O cluster calculations. This can be done by replacing the EEM charging dynamics with ACKS2 [36], which has the potential to better describe the charging boundary conditions of the impact H particle and, thus, a better description of the chemistry at the top layer of the surface. In the case of the amorphous LiOH (a:LiOH) surface, an impacting H atom acquires a balanced number of positive and negative charges, which create with the resident atoms water, OH radicals, lithium-hydride, and hydrogen molecules, and likely takes a part in recreating LiOH molecules. This picture is qualitatively similar to the one obtained by the QCMD/DFTB approach. Since the process of accumulation of hydrogen in the surface changes its content by both volumetric concentration and by a possible chain of chemical processes described here, it is important for a final understanding of these processes to consider the chemical evolution of the surface during H accumulation, which will be a subject of our future research.
